what_its_for: Verapamil is used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and certain heart rhythm problems. It belongs to a group of medicines called calcium channel blockers. It works by relaxing your blood vessels and slowing your heart rate so your heart does not have to work as hard.
how_to_take: Take verapamil exactly as your doctor prescribed. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food or milk may help if it upsets your stomach. Swallow extended-release tablets or capsules whole — do not crush, chew, or break them. If you have a capsule that your doctor said you can open, you may sprinkle the contents on a spoonful of applesauce and swallow it right away without chewing. Always take your doses at the same time each day to keep a steady level of medicine in your body.
dosing: Your dose will be set by your doctor based on your condition and how your body responds to the medicine. Doses are usually taken 1 to 3 times a day depending on the form you are prescribed. Common starting doses range from 40 mg to 120 mg per dose. Extended-release forms are usually taken once or twice a day. Never change your dose or stop taking verapamil without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store verapamil at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking grapefruit juice while taking verapamil — it can increase the amount of medicine in your blood and raise the risk of side effects. Avoid alcohol, as it can lower your blood pressure too much and make you feel dizzy. Do not drive or use heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, since it may cause dizziness or light-headedness. Tell your doctor before taking any new medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements, especially St. John's Wort, as many drugs can interact with verapamil.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you have: a very slow heartbeat (below 60 beats per minute), severe dizziness or fainting, shortness of breath or difficulty breathing, swelling in your legs or ankles, chest pain that is new or getting worse, yellowing of your skin or eyes (signs of liver problems), or unusual tiredness or weakness. Also contact your doctor if your blood pressure readings are consistently too high or too low.
when_it_works: For high blood pressure, verapamil may start lowering your blood pressure within the first 1 to 2 hours after taking a dose, but it may take 1 to 2 weeks of regular use before you feel the full benefit. For heart rhythm problems and chest pain, improvement may also be noticed within the first few days. Keep taking your medicine even if you feel well — stopping suddenly can make your condition worse.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and older): You may be more sensitive to verapamil's effects such as dizziness and low blood pressure. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before using verapamil if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Verapamil passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney or liver disease: Your dose may need to be adjusted. Always tell your doctor about all your health conditions before starting this medicine.
